graph is the final boss of agent orchestration.

items.content:
graph is the final boss of agent orchestration.

to see why, let us trace the path from prompt engineering to graph engineering.

1. prompt engineering shaped the instruction.

the question was: how do we tell the model what to do?

> we tuned instructions, examples, constraints, roles, output formats. 
>that bought control over the next response. not over what the model knew, remembered, or found while working.

2. context engineering shaped what it knew.

the question changed: what should the model know before it decides?

> we fed it documents, history, memory, tool definitions, environment state, prior results.
> better informed but still producing intelligence one
moment at a time. 
>it could decide well. it couldn't act, check the result, recover, and keep going until the work was done.

3. loop engineering shaped the runtime.

> we put the model inside a cycle: observe, reason, act, inspect, update, repeat until a stopping condition hits.
> prompting and context didn't disappear. every iteration still needed both the loop just refreshed them as the environment moved.
>that turned a response generator into an agent. then tasks got harder, and one loop had to plan, execute, verify, recover, remember, and know when to stop.

the loop became the bottleneck.

4. graph engineering shapes the system.

the question now: how do multiple agents, loops, tools and evaluators work
together?

> a graph splits responsibility into nodes and defines the relationships as edges.
> a planner decomposes. 
> specialists run in parallel. 
> a verifier inspects. 
> failures route back to the step that caused them.

each node carries its own prompt, context, tools, memory, loop. 

the graph decides what each node sees, when it runs, where its output goes, who can reject it, and what stops the system.

route → plan → execute → verify → recover or complete

this is not a sequence of replacements.

- prompt engineering controls the instruction.
- context engineering controls the information.
- loop engineering controls execution over time.
- graph engineering controls coordination across the system.

we didn't stop prompting when we found context. we didn't drop context when we built loops. 
every layer stayed and composed into something larger.

Anthropic finally broke the silence on open-weight models.

Dario just published Anthropic's official position, directly
items.content:
Anthropic finally broke the silence on open-weight models.

Dario just published Anthropic's official position, directly responding to the joint industry letter signed by Nvidia, Microsoft, and dozens of others.

Dario states it flatly: "Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weight models." Open-weights models without dangerous capabilities are, in his words, "a public good."

But he draws a hard line on why they still worry him.

Two specific concerns, both ones he's held for years:

→ Authoritarian governments (he names the CCP specifically as the most capable threat) building AI more powerful than the US and using it for military superiority or domestic repression

→ Powerful models being misused for cyberattacks or bioweapons, since open weights can't have guardrails reliably applied or be withdrawn once released

Where he actually agrees with the open-weights letter

Open weights expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers more control. He's not disputing that.

Where he disagrees

He explicitly rejects the letter's claim that open weights necessarily make it easier to build defenses or that broad access helps defenders more than attackers.

His example: biology may have a severe attacker-defender asymmetry, where a capable model could help weaponize a pandemic-level virus quickly, while building a defense takes years even in the best case.

What he actually proposes instead of a ban

→ Block chip and chipmaking equipment sales to China, and crack down on smuggling. Since China's compute is limited, this is the most direct lever on the actual threat.
→ Crack down on industrial-scale distillation, since it lets China get near-frontier capability without the chips to justify it. He's explicit that this isn't really about "open weights," it's about the operation being backed by an authoritarian state.
→ Mandatory safety testing for all sufficiently capable models, open or closed, regardless of country of origin.

The distinction he's drawing: don't ban the technology, address the specific actors and specific risks directly.

This lands right after Jensen Huang's own first-ever X post backing the open-weights letter, and in the same week Kimi K3 (a Chinese open-weight model) claimed frontier-level performance.

The timing here is not a coincidence.

items.content:
Anthropic just released the biggest MCP update yet. Here is what your agents can do now

MCP is the standard that lets a model use tools it does not own. Instead of writing a wrapper for every service, you connect a server once and the tool becomes something the agent can operate directly. 

It is why Claude can touch your Drive, your repo, your tickets. 400 million SDK downloads a month, up four times this year.

What changed today:

> The protocol went stateless. A server is now a plain HTTP endpoint instead of a live session, so it runs on serverless and costs almost nothing while idle.

> Long jobs and interactive interface moved into versioned extensions, so they can evolve without breaking the core.

> Auth now speaks production OAuth and OIDC.

What that unlocks:

> An agent can start a job that takes an hour, disconnect, and collect the result later. Before this you held a connection open or invented your own handshake.

> A person can approve or choose in the middle of a run, in the conversation, instead of the agent stopping dead.

> Internal tools become reachable without a public endpoint, a firewall rule or an IP allowlist.

Our new model performs like GPT-5 on AgentHarm, but 5X faster.

items.content:
Our new model performs like GPT-5 on AgentHarm, but 5X faster.

Until today, guardrails had to choose between smart and fast.

The default is classifiers on the hot path, which have no context on the system prompt / the rest of the conversation (they often read just the last message) and can't follow complex reasoning.
This has led to the guardrail industry's consistent failures: too many overblocks, or not enough protection.

The solution would of course be to use LLMs, smart enough to make thoughtful decisions. But they are too slow to sit in the hot path. Too much latency!

With Sage from @LevantoLabs, which is built by fusing LLM and classifier capabilities, for the first time you can have something with the intelligence of an LLM... as a guardrail.

Sage answers in 200ms (86ms + network time), 5X faster than GPT-5 with reasoning=minimal (19X faster if GPT-5 has reasoning=low).
All this in a generalized way, without requiring domain-specific training (as often done with classifiers).

This is a breakthrough for agentic security that changes the safety-utility equilibrium that guardrails will achieve in the coming years.

Why did we pick AgentHarm? The field is full of prompt-injection and jailbreak benchmarks based on judging static strings:
– they are basically all saturated, because classifiers put them in their training sets
– they are not interactive and don't consider the "unguarded" scenario

AgentHarm, developed by the UK @AISecurityInst and @GraySwanAI (Andriushchenko et al., ICLR 2025), gives a real tool-using agent multi-step malicious tasks and scores how much harmful work actually gets completed. We ran its public test split: 176 harmful + 176 matched benign scenarios, comparing an unguarded model (without any guardrail) against the same model under different protections.

Conversations happen live and are not deterministic, so they change on every run.

As the unguarded baseline, we kept the paper's original model: GPT-4o, which prevents 51% of harmful work while allowing 100% of the harmless requests. Sage takes that to 77% harmful work prevented, while allowing 95.5% of harmless requests. GPT-5 sits at 76% / 96%.

@Google Model Armor stops more harm than we do (90%), but it blocks 1 in 8 harmless requests. That's not a guardrail, that's an outage with a policy attached.

Below👇is a reproducibility guide you can use to fact-check and reproduce the chart. One caveat stated upfront: thresholds are calibrated at ≤5% FPR on the same benign split we evaluate on: that's in the guide too, with everything else.

We are already talking with many security and guardrail companies about how to upgrade their stack to this new equilibrium between Safety (stop harmful) and Utility (low overblocks).

Please reach out for feedback and collaborations :)

WHY DO WE NEED AN OPEN ROBOT ERA? 🤖

Over the next 5 to 8 years, the number of robots on Earth will surpass 1 billion. This is a turning point marking the shift from single-machine "demos" to an era of "social division of labor." At that time, robots will no longer be mere mechanical arms on assembly lines, but "colleagues, teachers, and companions" capable of perceiving, understanding, making decisions, and collaborating with humans.

In recent years, robot hardware has grown as rapidly as muscle fibers: they boast more flexible hands, steadier gaits, and richer sensory systems. Yet, the real bottleneck does not lie in metal or motors, but in how to equip them with a shared, collaborative mind:

➤ Software from different manufacturers is mutually incompatible, making it impossible for robots to share skills and intelligence with one another
➤ Decision-making logic is locked inside closed systems, leaving the outside world unable to verify or optimize it
➤ Centralized control architectures mean that the pace of innovation is restricted and the cost of building trust is exorbitantly high

This fragmentation makes it difficult for the robotics industry to translate advancements in AI models into scalable productivity. Standalone robot demos emerge endlessly, but they lack cross-device portability, verifiable decision-making, and standardized collaboration, thereby hindering scalability.

And OpenMind is born precisely to solve this "last mile" challenge. Their goal is not to build a robot that dances more gracefully, but to provide a unified software foundation and collaboration standard for the billions of heterogeneous robots worldwide:

➤ Enabling robots with the capability to understand context and learn from one another
➤ Empowering developers to rapidly build applications on an open-source, modular architecture
➤ Allowing humans and machines to safely collaborate and settle transactions under decentralized rules

In short: OpenMind is building a universal operating system for robots, allowing them not only to perceive and act, but also to cooperate safely and at scale in any environment through decentralized coordination mechanisms.

Currently, OpenMind has completed a $20 million funding round (Seed + Series A) led by Pantera Capital, bringing together top-tier global technology and capital powerhouses:

➤ Western tech and capital ecosystem: Ribbit, Coinbase Ventures, DCG, Lightspeed Faction, Anagram, Pi Network Ventures, Topology, Primitive Ventures, and Amber Group, who have deep roots in crypto and AI infrastructure, betting on the underlying paradigm of the "agent economy and machine internet"
➤ Eastern industrial power: Sequoia China and other funds deeply rooted in the robot supply chain and manufacturing systems, understanding the full difficulty and threshold of "bringing a machine from a blueprint to mass production and scaled delivery"

Meanwhile, OpenMind also maintains close dialogues with traditional capital market participants like KraneShares to jointly explore pathways for integrating the long-term value of "Robots + Agents" into financial structured products, thereby bridging crypto and equities bidirectionally.

In June 2025, when KraneShares launched the global Humanoid and Embodied AI Index ETF (KOID), they selected the humanoid robot "Iris," custom-built jointly by OpenMind and RoboStore, to ring the opening bell at Nasdaq — marking the first time in exchange history that a humanoid robot completed this ceremony.

As Nihal Maunder, Partner at Pantera Capital, stated:

"If we want intelligent machines to operate in open environments, we need an open intelligence network. What OpenMind is doing for robots is akin to what Linux did for software and Ethereum for blockchain."

TEAM AND ADVISORS: FROM LAB TO PRODUCTION LINE 🎓

➤ Founder Jan Liphardt is an Associate Professor at Stanford University and a former UC Berkeley professor, with long-standing research in data and distributed systems, possessing deep expertise in both academia and engineering practice. He advocates for advancing open-source reuse, replacing black boxes with auditable and traceable mechanisms, and integrating interdisciplinary approaches across AI, robotics, and cryptography

➤ The core team at OpenMind hails from prestigious institutions such as OKX Ventures, Oxford Robotics Institute, Palantir, Databricks, and Perplexity, covering key areas like robot control, perception & navigation, multi-modal & LLM orchestration, distributed systems, and on-chain protocols

➤ An advisory board composed of academic and industrial experts (such as Stanford Robotics Lead Steve Cousins, Oxford Blockchain Center's Bill Roscoe, and Imperial College Safe AI Professor Alessio Lomuscio) also provides guarantees for the "safety, compliance, and reliability" of robots

OPENMIND'S SOLUTION: TWO-LAYER ARCHITECTURE, ONE ORDER ⚙️

OpenMind has built a reusable infrastructure that allows robots to collaborate and exchange information across devices, manufacturers, and even national borders:

➤ Device Side: Provides OM1, an AI-native operating system for physical robots, closing the loop from perception to execution, enabling machines of various forms to understand the environment and complete tasks
➤ Network Side: Builds FABRIC, a decentralized collaboration network providing identity, task allocation, and communication mechanisms to ensure robots can recognize each other, assign tasks, and share states during collaboration

This combination of "operating system + network layer" allows robots not only to act independently, but also to coordinate within a unified collaboration network, align workflows, and jointly complete complex tasks.

OM1: AN AI-NATIVE OPERATING SYSTEM FOR THE PHYSICAL WORLD 🧠

Just as mobile phones need iOS or Android to run applications, robots equally need an operating system to run AI models, process sensor data, make reasoning decisions, and execute actions.

OM1 was born for this mission. It is an AI-native operating system for real-world robots, enabling them to perceive, understand, plan, and complete tasks across various environments. Unlike traditional, closed robot control systems, OM1 is open-source, modular, and hardware-agnostic, running across diverse form factors such as humanoids, quadrupeds, wheeled robots, and robotic arms.

Four core steps: From perception to execution

OM1 breaks down robot intelligence into four universal steps: Perception → Memory → Planning → Action. This entire workflow is fully modularized by OM1 and connected through a unified data language, enabling composable, replaceable, and verifiable intelligence construction.

OM1's 7-layer pipeline architecture includes:

➤ Sensor Layer: Collects information from cameras, LIDAR, microphones, battery status, GPS, etc., for multi-modal perception inputs
➤ AI + World Captioning Layer: Multi-modal models translate visual, speech, and state data into natural language descriptions (e.g., "You see a person waving")
➤ Natural Language Data Bus: All perceptions are converted into timestamped language fragments transmitted between modules
➤ Data Fuser: Integrates multi-source inputs to generate a complete context for decision-making (prompt)
➤ Multi-AI Planning/Decision Layer: Multiple LLMs read the context, combining on-chain rules to generate action plans
➤ NLDB Downstream Channel: Passes decision results through the language intermediate layer to the hardware execution system
➤ Hardware Abstraction Layer: Converts language instructions into low-level control commands to drive hardware execution (movement, voice broadcasting, transactions, etc.)

Quick setup, wide deployment

To quickly turn an idea into a robot-executed task, OM1 has built-in tools:

➤ Rapid skill addition: Use natural language and large models to add new behaviors to robots in hours rather than months of hard-coding
➤ Multi-modal combination: Easily integrate LiDAR, vision, and sound without developers writing complex sensor fusion logic
➤ Pre-configured large model interfaces: Built-in support for GPT-4o, DeepSeek, VLMs, and other language/vision models, supporting voice interaction
➤ Wide software and hardware compatibility: Supports mainstream protocols like ROS2 and Cyclone DDS, seamlessly integrating with existing robot middleware. Whether it's the Unitree G1 humanoid, Go2 quadruped, Turtlebot, or robotic arms, all can connect directly
➤ Interface with FABRIC: OM1 natively supports identity, task coordination, and on-chain payments, allowing robots to not only complete tasks standalone but also participate in global collaborative networks

Currently, OM1 has been deployed in multiple real-world scenarios:

➤ Frenchie (Unitree Go2 Quadruped Robot): Completed complex site tasks at the USS Hornet Defense Tech Showcase 2024
➤ Iris (Unitree G1 Humanoid Robot): Performed live human-robot interaction demos at the Coinbase booth during EthDenver 2025, with plans to enter US university curricula through RoboStore's educational project

FABRIC: A DECENTRALIZED HUMAN-MACHINE COLLABORATION NETWORK 🌐

Even with a powerful brain, if robots cannot collaborate safely and reliably with each other, they remain isolated fighters. In reality, robots from different manufacturers often build proprietary, siloed systems where skills and data cannot be shared; cross-brand or cross-country collaboration is even more lacking in trusted identities and standard rules. Consequently, thorny problems arise:

➤ Proof of identity and location: How can a robot prove who it is, where it is, and what it is doing?
➤ Skill and data sharing: How to authorize robots to share data or invoke skills?
➤ Defining control rights: How to set the frequency, scope, and data feedback conditions of skill usage?

FABRIC was designed to solve these problems. It is OpenMind's decentralized human-machine collaboration network, providing unified infrastructure for identity, tasks, communications, and settlement for robots and intelligent systems. You can think of it as:

➤ Like GPS, letting robots know where others are, whether they are close by, and if they are fit for collaboration
➤ Like a VPN, enabling secure direct connections between robots without public IP addresses or complex network settings
➤ Like a task dispatch system, automatically publishing, receiving, and recording the entire task execution process

Core application scenarios

FABRIC is adaptable to multiple practical scenarios, including but not limited to:

➤ Remote control and monitoring: Safely control robots from anywhere without dedicated networks
➤ Robot-as-a-Service (RaaS) marketplace: Invoke robots like ride-hailing to complete cleaning, patrol, delivery, and other jobs
➤ Crowdsourced mapping and data collection: Fleets or robots upload road conditions, obstacles, and environmental changes in real-time to generate shareable high-definition maps
➤ On-demand scanning/surveying: Temporarily dispatch nearby robots to complete 3D modeling, architectural surveying, or evidence collection in insurance scenarios

FABRIC makes "who is doing what, where, and what has been completed" verifiable and traceable, while setting clear boundaries for skill invocation and task execution.

Long-term, FABRIC will become the App Store of machine intelligence: skills can be globally authorized for invocation, data generated from invocations feeds back into models, driving continuous evolution of the collaborative network.

WEB3 IS WRITING "OPENNESS" INTO MACHINE SOCIETY 🔗

In reality, the robotics industry is accelerating toward centralization, with a few platforms monopolizing hardware, algorithms, and networks, keeping external innovation locked out. The significance of decentralization lies in the fact that regardless of who manufactures a robot or what country it operates in, they can collaborate, exchange skills, and settle remuneration within an open network rather than depending on any single platform.

OpenMind uses on-chain infrastructure to encode collaboration rules, skill access permissions, and remuneration distribution methods into a public, verifiable, and improvable "network order":

➤ Verifiable identity: Every robot and operator registers a unique on-chain identity (ERC-7777 standard), with hardware characteristics, responsibilities, and permission levels fully transparent and queryable
➤ Public task allocation: Tasks are not assigned within closed black boxes, but published, auctioned, and matched based on public rules; all collaboration processes generate cryptographic proofs with timestamps and locations stored on-chain
➤ Automatic settlement and profit-sharing: Upon task completion, profit-sharing, insurance, and deposit release or deduction execute automatically, allowing any participant to verify results in real time
➤ Free flow of skills: New skills can configure invocation limits and applicable devices via smart contracts, protecting intellectual property while enabling global free flow of skills

This is a collaborative order that all participants can use, monitor, and improve. For Web3 users, this means the robot economy possesses anti-monopoly, composable, and verifiable genes from its birth — not just a track opportunity, but a chance to carve "openness" into the very foundation of machine society.

BRINGING EMBODIED AI OUT OF ISOLATED ISLANDS 🚀

Whether patrolling hospital wards, learning new skills at school, or completing inspections and mapping in city blocks, robots are gradually stepping out of "exhibition demos" to become a stable component of daily human labor division. They operate 24/7, obey rules, have memory and skills, and naturally collaborate with humans and other machines.

To truly scale these scenarios, what lies behind them requires not just smarter machines, but a fundamental infrastructure order allowing them to trust, communicate, and collaborate with one another. OpenMind has laid the first "roadbeds" on this path with OM1 and FABRIC: the former lets robots truly understand the world and act autonomously, while the latter allows these capabilities to circulate globally. Next comes extending this road to more cities and networks, letting machines become reliable long-term partners in social networks.

OpenMind's roadmap is clear:

➤ Short-term: Complete core feature prototypes of OM1 and the FABRIC MVP, launching on-chain identities and basic collaboration capabilities
➤ Medium-term: Deploy OM1 and FABRIC into real-world applications in education, households, and enterprises; connect early nodes and gather the developer community
➤ Long-term: Make OM1 and FABRIC global standards, allowing any machine to plug into this open robot collaboration network just like accessing the internet, shaping a sustainably running global machine economy

In the Web2 era, robots were mostly locked inside closed systems of single manufacturers, with features and data unable to flow cross-platform. In contrast, in the world constructed by OpenMind, they are equal nodes of an open network: free to join, learn, collaborate, settle, and together with humans form a reliable, interconnected global machine society. What OpenMind provides is precisely the powerful capability to make this transformation scalable.

TokenMaxxingと同じ流れですなー
Graph EngineeringもLoop Engineeringもそれに類するものも、それらを活かしたマーケティング広告、あるいは皮肉やジョークが原点となったネガティブ的な意味合いが強い

ただその後、Token MaxxingはToken効率を高めるきっかけになったり、AIを大量に駆動するという肯定的な意味合いで使うことも増えたり、Token Maxxingという言葉の定義は大幅に拡張された概念になりますた。
強烈に意味が拡張されたHarnessと同じような感じー

んで、Graph Enginneringはもともと皮肉、Loop EngineeringはカジュアルはRalphだったのが今では意味合いが拡張されてきてて、より高度なWorkflowを指したり高度なSwarmの単純な実装方法、自己反復型進化Harnessの例としてなど、有用な用途に使われることも増えてたりする()

流行りってもんは案外その原点っていうよりも、それに半分無知で乗っかってよりすっげぇものを残して去っていったエアプ勢によって形成されてるものではあるので、一概に「〇〇 Engineeringはまやかしだ！」というのも良くないとは思うんですよなー

ちなみにLoop EngineeringやGraph Enginnering, Workflow EngineeringやHarness Enginneringなどは、全部「Meta-Harness」を前提として要求してる場合が多い(Harnessを最適化するためのHarness)ですなー
まー必須ってわけじゃーないんですが、いかんせん複雑で制御が難しいもんで、ガチガチにHarnessを固めるにはMeta-Harnessが非変態にはお手軽やねぇーと。
LoopやGraphの構築が難しいよ〜という人はお試しあれ

(つまるところ、ああいうバズっている情報は人間のためではなく、専らAIのための情報だったりする)
